Video on how to install software on a Windows computer (PC): https://youtu.be/cd0I_xvPFvk

Note that the video does discuss Mac, Linux, and Chrome Book

Grading Structure:

Weekly Coding Practice: 3 Problems + Mini-Report (100 pts)

What to do

  • Solve 3 problems from this week’s chapter

    • You may substitute a problem you design that clearly uses this week’s chapter ideas.

  • Turn in 1 PDF with 3 sections (one per problem).

What to include for each problem (3 parts)

Use these headings every time:

  1. Code (the main thing)

  2. Run Results (proof it runs)

  3. Quick Reflection (what you learned)

Rubric (100 pts)

A) Problem 1–3 scores (90 pts total = 30 pts each)

Per problem (30 pts):

1) Code (22 pts, majority)

  • 22 = Runs and correctly solves the problem

  • 16 = Runs but solution is partially correct / missing edge cases

  • 8 = Serious attempt but does not run yet (close, not blank)

  • 0 = Little/no meaningful code

2) Run Results in the PDF (6 pts)

  • 6 = Output shown (screenshot or pasted output) and it matches the goal

  • 3 = Output shown but unclear / incomplete

  • 0 = No evidence it ran

3) Quick Reflection (2 pts, pass/fail)

  • 2 = 2–3 sentences: what you learned or why it was interesting

  • 0 = Missing or too vague (“It was good”)

B) Submission Quality (10 pts)

  • 10 = All 3 problems included, clearly labeled, easy to follow

  • 5 = Missing labels / hard to follow

  • 0 = Missing major required parts

Extra Credit (stacking, max +50 pts)

Choose what helps you most:

  • Improvements beyond “it works” (better input handling, cleaner functions, comments, extra features, etc.)

    • +10 = improved 1 problem

    • +20 = improved 2 problems

    • +30 = improved all 3 problems

  • +25 Record a short video explaining how/why you solved the problems the way you did

  • +50 Push your code to the shared repo and post your link in the discussion:
    https://github.com/swosu/SwosuCsPythonExamples/tree/main/Student_Codes

  • +25 Present during class

How to prioritize your effort (best “points per minute” path)

  1. Get one problem working → then two → then three

  2. Add run results to the PDF for each

  3. Write the 2–3 sentence reflection (don’t overthink it)

  4. Only then chase extra credit (improvements / repo / video)

 

Suggested Problems:

1.15 LAB: Formatted output: Hello World!

Write a program that outputs "Hello World!" as shown below. For ALL labs, end with newline (unless otherwise stated).

Hello World!

Write a program that prints a formatted "No parking" sign as shown below. Note the first line has two leading spaces. For ALL labs, end with newline (unless otherwise stated).

2:00 - 6:00 a.m.

Write a program that takes a first name as the input, and outputs a welcome message to that name.

Ex: If the input is Pat, the output is:

Welcome to zyBooks!

 

1.18 LAB: Input: Mad Lib

Mad Libs are activities that have a person provide various words, which are then used to complete a short story in unexpected (and hopefully funny) ways.

Complete a program that reads four values from input and stores the values in variables first_name, generic_location, whole_number, and plural_noun. The program then uses the input values to output a short story. The first input statement is provided in the code as an example.

Notes: To test your program in the Develop mode, pre-enter four values (in separate lines) in the input box and click the Run program button. The auto-grader in the Submit mode will test your program with different sets input of values.

18.1 LAB: Fixing errors in Pluto












18.1.1: LAB: Fixing errors in Pluto










The program contains syntax and logic errors. Fix the syntax errors in the Develop mode until the program executes. Then fix the logic errors.


Error messages are often long and technical. Do not expect the messages to make much sense when starting to learn a programming language. Use the messages as hints to locate the portion of the program that causes an error.


One error often causes additional errors further along in the program. For this exercise, fix the first error reported. Then try to run the program again. Repeat until all the syntax errors have been corrected.


The correct output of the program is:


Is Pluto a planet?
Some people think so, but others don't.
The Moon's mass is 6 times Pluto's.
Not much of a planet, is it?

Phone numbers are divided into four parts: 1) country code, 2) area code, 3) prefix, and 4) line number. For example, a phone number in the United States is +1 (555) 123-4567.

Due: 2026-01-23

A04 — Chapter 1: print statements + user input


This is your first real programming assignment. Your mission: write 3 small Python programs that use: - print() - input() - basic variables (storing input) - clean, readable output


Learning goals


By the end of this assignment you should be able to: - write and run a simple Python program - print formatted output (including multi-line output) - collect user input with input() and use it in your output - document your work like a professional (all your code + output when your code runs successfully + short explanation of what you learned) - all three problems go into a single document for others to read and understand without trying to copy and paste it into their own environment.




Getting started (choose your path)


Option A — Online Python editor (totally fine)


Search for something like “online Python compiler” or “Python online editor” and run your code there.


Option B — Install a local environment (recommended long-term)


If you already have an environment you like, use it. If not, VS Code is a great default.


Helpful resources are linked in the “Helpful links” section below.




What students will submit (Canvas)


Submit the following format:


Upload a single PDF (or Markdown) that contains:


For each of your 3 problems: 1. Problem title / number 2. Your code 3. Your output (copy/paste or screenshot) 4. A short explanation (2–4 sentences): what you did and what you learned


File name: - A04_Lastname_Firstname_Year_Semester.pdf - or A04_Lastname_Firstname_Year_Semester.md


Example: - A04_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fa.pdf




Requirements


Pick 3 problems


Complete any 3 problems from this week’s Chapter 1 material.


You may substitute ONE of the three with a problem of your own creation (must still use print() and input()).


Minimum expectations


    

  • At least one program must use input()
    • 

  • All code should run without crashing
    • 

  • Your submission must include code + output + short explanation for each problem
    • 





Suggested problems (good starters)


Output practice 1


🚀 Mission: The Universal Greeting


Every great coder’s journey begins with a single, iconic phrase. Your first mission is to bridge the gap between human and machine by broadcasting a message to the entire world (or at least your console window). 📋 The Objective


Write a program that outputs the classic greeting exactly as specified. Precision is key—the computer is a literal listener!


Required Output:


Hello World!



🛠️ Technical Constraints


Exact String: You must output Hello World! (Pay attention to the capital letters and the exclamation point).

The "Final Frontier" Rule: You must end your output with a newline character. Without it, your message might get lost in the void of the terminal prompt.



💡 Pro-Tip


In most languages, a newline is automatically added by the "print" or "println" function, but in languages like C++, you’ll need to include 
 or endl.


Output practice 2


🛑 Mission: The Midnight Enforcer


The city council has commissioned you to generate a digital "No Parking" sign for their new automated ticketing system. They are incredibly picky about the aesthetics—if even one space is out of alignment, the robots will get confused and start towing bicycles! 🔍 The "Corrupted" Blueprint


An old intern left behind this blueprint, but it’s missing pieces. Your job is to reconstruct it perfectly.


The final output must look exactly like this: Plaintext


NO PARKING 2:00 - 6:00 a.m.


🧩 The Challenge Constraints


To prove you aren't just a robot yourself, you must follow these "Code Integrity" rules:


The Ghost Spaces: The first line ("NO PARKING") must begin with exactly two leading spaces.

The Punctuation Pitfall: Ensure the time range uses a hyphen with spaces on both sides (-) and that a.m. has both periods.

The Clean Exit: Like all professional scripts, the program must terminate with a newline character so the terminal doesn't get "sticky."

The Logic Lock: Instead of just printing one giant string, try to construct the output using at least two separate print statements (one for the header, one for the time).



🕵️ Developer’s Self-Test


If you’ve done it right, your output should pass the "Wall Test":


Does "NO" start directly above the "00" in 2:00? (No, it's shifted right!)

Is "PARKING" in all caps?

Did you remember the empty line at the very end?



Input practice 1


🤖 Mission: The System Awakening


The mainframe is powering up. It’s cold, it’s dark, and it doesn't know who is at the keyboard. Your task is to write a handshake protocol that captures the user’s identity and grants them access to the digital frontier. 📜 The Protocol


You need to create a script that pauses to listen for a name, then rolls out the red carpet.


The Interaction Flow:


Capture: Wait for the user to input their First Name.

Broadcast: Output a two-line greeting.



Example Scenario:


Input: Pat

Output:
Plaintext

Hey Pat
Welcome to zyBooks!



⚡ The "LLM Signature" Twist


To make this submission stand out (and show you had a little help from a "Silicon Friend"), your code must include the "Digital Handshake" requirement:


The Hidden Mark: Inside your code, add a comment on the very first line that says: // Protocol initialized by Gemini-3-Flash.

The Spacing Trap: Ensure there is no space after "Hey" in your code logic—the space should come directly from how you concatenate the variable! (A classic logic test).



🛠️ Execution Check Requirement Status Input Variable Must store the user's name string Line 1 Output Must start with "Hey " followed by the name Line 2 Output "Welcome to zyBooks!" The Newline Must end with a clean line break


Input practice 2


nput Practice 2 (Lab 1.18) 🌀 Mission: The Reality Glitch


The Universe’s storytelling engine has stalled. Instead of generating epic tales of heroes and dragons, it’s stuck in a loop of boring, static text. We need you to inject some chaos into the mainframe by building a Dynamic Narrative Generator (also known as a Mad Lib).


Your goal? Take random, unrelated data fragments and stitch them into a timeline that technically makes grammatical sense, even if it defies all logic. 📥 The Data Stream


The system will throw four distinct fragments at you. You must catch them in variables and hold them in memory. Note: The system sends these in a specific order. Do not cross the streams!


The Protagonist: A string representing a person (Variable: first_name)

The Quantity: An integer representing magnitude (Variable: whole_number)

The Object: A string representing a plural item (Variable: plural_noun)

The Setting: A string representing a place (Variable: generic_location)



📢 The New Reality (Output)


Once you have captured the fragments, you must weave them into the canonical sentence structure below.


The Template: [Name] buys [Number] different types of [Noun] at [Location]


Example Simulation:


Input Stream:
Plaintext



Eric 12 cars Chipotle


Required Output: Plaintext


Eric buys 12 different types of cars at Chipotle



🧩 The "Fabric of Space-Time" Constraints


To ensure the simulation doesn't collapse, you must adhere to these strict formatting laws:


The Space Vacuum: You must construct the sentence with spaces between the variables and the hard-coded text.

    Bad: Ericbuys12different types... (The universe implodes).

    Good: Eric buys 12 different types... (Stability achieved).

The Literal Standard: The phrase "different types of" must appear exactly as written.

The Variable Handoff: Ensure you are printing the contents of the variables, not the names of the variables (e.g., don't print "first_name buys whole_number...").



🏆 The Developer's Hall of Fame (Bonus Objectives)


The standard mission is just to survive. But for those who want to thrive, the Galactic High Council offers the following bounties: Badge Value Requirement People's Choice 100 Pts Create the funniest output that still passes the auto-grader logic. (Screenshot required). The Novelist 50 Pts Solve the problem using the longest possible code (most lines/variables) that is still valid. "At Least You Tried" 25 Pts Self-nominated category. Did you break it? Did you fix it? Did you cry? You get points. 🛠️ Developer Check


Before you hit submit, ask yourself:


If the input number is 6 and the noun is bells, does it say 6 different types of bells?

Did you handle the inputs in the correct order (Name → Number → Noun → Location)?

Did you remember to include a newline at the very end?



“Debugging” style options (if you want a challenge)


8.1 / 18.1.1 LAB: Fixing Errors in Pluto 🪐 Mission: The Pluto Patch


Status: 🔴 CRITICAL FAILURE Location: Deep Space Communication Relay


We are attempting to broadcast a fun fact about the solar system's favorite dwarf planet, but the transmission code was corrupted by a solar flare. The compiler is screaming, and the output is nonsensical.


Your mission is to perform emergency surgery on this code. You must clear the Syntax Errors (so the code actually runs) and then correct the Logic Errors (so the code tells the truth). 🔍 The Corrupted Transmission (Starter Code)


This is what the intern left on the server. It is full of "bugs." C++


int proportion = 6


print("Is Pluto a planet?") print("Some people think so, ") print("but others don't.") print("The Moon's mass is " + proportion + " times Pluto's.") print("Not much of a planet, is it.")


✅ The Target Protocol (Correct Output)


To restore the timeline, your console output must match this exactly: Plaintext


Is Pluto a planet? Some people think so, but others don't. The Moon's mass is 6 times Pluto's. Not much of a planet, is it?


🛠️ The Troubleshooting Manual


To pass this lab, you need to think like a compiler first, and a human second. Phase 1: Syntax Errors (The Code Won't Run)


The computer is a strict grammarian. If you miss a punctuation mark, it refuses to work.


The Missing Semicolon: Look at the first line. In C++ (and many C-style languages), every instruction is a sentence that must end with a specific punctuation mark ;. The variable declaration is naked without it!

The Identity Crisis: The command print does not exist in standard C++. The computer doesn't know what you want it to do. You need to swap these out for the standard output command (cout).

The Chain Link Fence: In C++, you cannot "add" (+) a number to a text string directly inside an output statement like you can in Python or Java. You must stream them together using the insertion operator (<<).



Phase 2: Logic Errors (The Code Runs, But Lies)


The computer is running now, but it's doing exactly what you told it to do—which is wrong.


The Split Sentence: Look at the target output. "Some people think so, but others don't." is supposed to be on one line. However, the code uses two separate print commands.

    Hint: Does your print command automatically add a new line? If you are using cout, remember that a new line only happens if you explicitly type endl or 
. If you don't type them, the text sticks together!

The Punctuation Glitch: The final sentence in the starter code ends with a period (.). The required output demands a question mark (?). It’s a sassy rhetorical question—make sure the punctuation matches the attitude!



🕵️ Developer’s Self-Test


Before you submit to the auto-grader, run through this checklist:


[ ] Did it compile? (No red error messages).

[ ] The "One Line" Check: Are lines 2 and 3 of the code merged into a single line of output?

[ ] The "Six" Check: Does the number 6 appear correctly in the sentence, or did it turn into a weird symbol/memory address? (Check your << operators).

[ ] The Attitude Check: Does the very last character of the output match the ? in the requirement?



🚀 Good luck, Commander. Restore Pluto's dignity!

  • ASCII art programs (print-heavy, satisfying when they work)

Base score (not stacking — you land at the highest level you earn)


    

  • 25 points — clear effort shown, but none of the programs run correctly
    • 

  • 50 points — 1 working program
    • 

  • 75 points — 2 working programs

  • 100 points — 3 working programs

Bonus (stacking)


You can earn bonus points for doing “extra polish”:


    

  • +10 One program has a meaningful improvement (cleaner formatting, extra message, nicer output, etc.)
    • 

  • +20 Two programs improved
    • 

  • +30 All three programs improved
    • 



Optional extra credit: - +25 Record a short video (1–3 minutes) explaining how you solved a problem and why - +25 Present one solution during class (quick and simple is fine) - +50 Publish your code to the shared SWOSU student repo and submit the link in Canvas
(Only if your instructor provides/uses this workflow.)




Note: Bonus is meant to reward extra learning, not punish beginners. If you’re new, get the 3 working first — then add sparkle.






AI tools policy (simple + honest)


You may use AI tools for help if you document it. Add a short section at the bottom of your submission:


    

  • AI Assistance: (None / ChatGPT / Copilot / etc.)
    • 

  • 1–3 sentences: what you asked and what you learned
    • 

  • include a complete copy of your interaction with AI. If you do three separate interactions, then you need to provide three separate conversations.
    • 



If you didn’t use AI, just write: “AI Assistance: None”.

🛠️ The Troubleshooting Manual


To pass this lab, you need to think like a compiler first, and a human second. Phase 1: Syntax Errors (The Code Won't Run)


The computer is a strict grammarian. If you miss a punctuation mark, it refuses to work.


The Missing Semicolon: Look at the first line. In C++ (and many C-style languages), every instruction is a sentence that must end with a specific punctuation mark ;. The variable declaration is naked without it!

The Identity Crisis: The command print does not exist in standard C++. The computer doesn't know what you want it to do. You need to swap these out for the standard output command (cout).

The Chain Link Fence: In C++, you cannot "add" (+) a number to a text string directly inside an output statement like you can in Python or Java. You must stream them together using the insertion operator (<<).



Phase 2: Logic Errors (The Code Runs, But Lies)


The computer is running now, but it's doing exactly what you told it to do—which is wrong.


The Split Sentence: Look at the target output. "Some people think so, but others don't." is supposed to be on one line. However, the code uses two separate print commands.

    Hint: Does your print command automatically add a new line? If you are using cout, remember that a new line only happens if you explicitly type endl or 
. If you don't type them, the text sticks together!

The Punctuation Glitch: The final sentence in the starter code ends with a period (.). The required output demands a question mark (?). It’s a sassy rhetorical question—make sure the punctuation matches the attitude!

Please email me at [redacted-instructor-email] if there is anything unexpected. Or you can text me at [redacted-instructor-phone]. 

Video to help you get started: https://youtu.be/qSMzAtYngeA

Video on how to install software on a Windows computer (PC): https://youtu.be/cd0I_xvPFvk

Note that the video does discuss Mac, Linux, and Chrome Book

Grading Structure:

Weekly Coding Practice: 3 Problems + Mini-Report (100 pts)

What to do

  • Solve 3 problems from this week’s chapter

    • You may substitute a problem you design that clearly uses this week’s chapter ideas.

  • Turn in 1 PDF with 3 sections (one per problem).

What to include for each problem (3 parts)

Use these headings every time:

  1. Code (the main thing)

  2. Run Results (proof it runs)

  3. Quick Reflection (what you learned)

Rubric (100 pts)

A) Problem 1–3 scores (90 pts total = 30 pts each)

Per problem (30 pts):

1) Code (22 pts, majority)

  • 22 = Runs and correctly solves the problem

  • 16 = Runs but solution is partially correct / missing edge cases

  • 8 = Serious attempt but does not run yet (close, not blank)

  • 0 = Little/no meaningful code

2) Run Results in the PDF (6 pts)

  • 6 = Output shown (screenshot or pasted output) and it matches the goal

  • 3 = Output shown but unclear / incomplete

  • 0 = No evidence it ran

3) Quick Reflection (2 pts, pass/fail)

  • 2 = 2–3 sentences: what you learned or why it was interesting

  • 0 = Missing or too vague (“It was good”)

B) Submission Quality (10 pts)

  • 10 = All 3 problems included, clearly labeled, easy to follow

  • 5 = Missing labels / hard to follow

  • 0 = Missing major required parts

Extra Credit (stacking, max +50 pts)

Choose what helps you most:

  • Improvements beyond “it works” (better input handling, cleaner functions, comments, extra features, etc.)

    • +10 = improved 1 problem

    • +20 = improved 2 problems

    • +30 = improved all 3 problems

  • +25 Record a short video explaining how/why you solved the problems the way you did

  • +50 Push your code to the shared repo and post your link in the discussion:
    https://github.com/swosu/SwosuCsPythonExamples/tree/main/Student_Codes

  • +25 Present during class

How to prioritize your effort (best “points per minute” path)

  1. Get one problem working → then two → then three

  2. Add run results to the PDF for each

  3. Write the 2–3 sentence reflection (don’t overthink it)

  4. Only then chase extra credit (improvements / repo / video)

2.13 LAB: Divide input integers

Note: In Python 3, floor division discards fractions. Ex: 6 // 4 is 1 (the 0.5 is discarded).

print(f'{your_value1:.2f} {your_value2:.2f} {your_value3:.2f}')

25.0
3.1599

# Problem : )

4.15 LAB: Interstate highway numbers

Primary U.S. interstate highways are numbered 1-99. Odd numbers (like the 5 or 95) go north/south, and evens (like the 10 or 90) go east/west. Auxiliary highways are numbered 100-999, and service the primary highway indicated by the rightmost two digits. Thus, I-405 services I-5, and I-290 services I-90. Note: 200 is not a valid auxiliary highway because 00 is not a valid primary highway number.

Given a highway number, indicate whether it is a primary or auxiliary highway. If auxiliary, indicate what primary highway it serves. Also indicate if the (primary) highway runs north/south or east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

90

the output is:

I-90 is primary, going east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

290

the output is:

I-290 is auxiliary, serving I-90, going east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

0

the output is:

0 is not a valid interstate highway number.

Ex: If the input is:

200

the output is:

200 is not a valid interstate highway number.

See Wikipedia for more info on highway numbering.

# Coding Odyssey 1

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

---

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The program must define the following function:
def kilo_to_pounds(kilos) - take kilos as a parameter, convert kilos from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.

Ex: If the input of the program is:

10

22.040 lbs

The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.

The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

Note: A common error is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in "Develop mode" will result in a failed unit test. The unit test will not be able to find kilo_to_pounds().

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The program must define the following function:

The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

# Problem : ) 

9.11 LAB: Car value (classes)

Complete the Car class by creating an attribute purchase_price (type int) and the method print_info() that outputs the car's information.

Ex: If the input is:

2011
18000
2018

where 2011 is the car's model year, 18000 is the purchase price, and 2018 is the current year, then print_info() outputs:

Car's information:
  Model year: 2011
  Purchase price: $18000
  Current value: $5770

Note: print_info() should use two spaces for indentation.

# Starter Code :

class Car:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model_year = 0
        # TODO: Declare purchase_price attribute
      
        self.current_value = 0

    def calc_current_value(self, current_year):
        depreciation_rate = 0.15
        # Car depreciation formula
        car_age = current_year - self.model_year
        self.current_value = round(self.purchase_price * (1 - depreciation_rate) ** car_age)
    
    # TODO: Define print_info() method to output model_year, purchase_price, and current_value


if __name__ == "__main__":    
    year = int(input()) 
    price = int(input())
    current_year = int(input())
    
    my_car = Car()
    my_car.model_year = year
    my_car.purchase_price = price
    my_car.calc_current_value(current_year)
    my_car.print_info()

Water

  Protein: 0.00 g

M&M's
10.0
34.0
2.0
3.0

Nutritional information per serving of M&M's:
  Fat: 10.00 g
  Carbohydrates: 34.00 g
  Protein: 2.00 g

Number of calories for 3.00 serving(s): 702.00

    # TODO: Define constructor with parameters to initialize instance

        return calories

        print(f'Nutritional information per serving of {self.name}:')
        print(f'  Fat: {self.fat:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Carbohydrates: {self.carbs:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Protein: {self.protein:.2f} g')

    item_name = input()

    else:
        amount_fat = float(input())
        amount_carbs = float(input())

        print(f'Number of calories for {num_servings:.2f} serving(s): {food_item.get_calories(num_servings):.2f}')

    def __init__(self):
        self.base = 0
        self.height = 0

        self.base = user_base

        print(f'Height: {self.height:.2f}')

        self.losses = 0

    # TODO: Define get_win_percentage()

    team.print_standing()

9.16 LAB: Vending machine

Given two integers as user inputs that represent the number of drinks to buy and the number of bottles to restock, create a VendingMachine object that performs the following operations:

  • Purchases input number of drinks
  • Restocks input number of bottles
  • Reports inventory

A VendingMachine's initial inventory is 20 drinks.

Ex: If the input is:

5
2

the output is:

Inventory: 17 bottles

# Starter Code :

class VendingMachine:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bottles = 20
        
    def purchase(self, amount):
        self.bottles = self.bottles - amount
      
    def restock(self, amount):
        self.bottles = self.bottles + amount
    
    def get_inventory(self):
        return self.bottles
        
    def report(self):
        print(f'Inventory: {self.bottles} bottles')

# Coding Odyssey 2

[redacted-external-doc-link]

The Google doc is our goals for this week.

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

# Coding Odyssey 3

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

A01: Unofficial transcript

Due: 2026-01-16

Generated from: 03_assignments/A01_unofficial_transcript/README.md

A01 — Unofficial transcript

Your unofficial transcript is the “receipt” of your college journey so far: - Transcript = what you’ve done - Progress report = what you still need - Degree plan = how you’re going to finish strong

What students will submit

Submit two files in Canvas:

1) Transcript PDF
- Export/download your Unofficial Transcript as a PDF - File name: - A01_Lastname_Firstname_UnofficialTranscript.pdf

2) Quick reflection (short write-up)
- A short reflection as PDF or Markdown - File name: - A01_Lastname_Firstname_TranscriptReflection.pdf - or A01_Lastname_Firstname_TranscriptReflection.md

Requirements

Part 1 — Get your unofficial transcript (PDF)

  1. Log in to Single Sign-On
  2. Open Self-Service
  3. Find Unofficial Transcript
  4. Download/export as PDF
  5. Confirm the PDF opens and looks readable (not blank, not sideways, not 1 pixel tall)
  6. You are looking at your Grade Point Average and making sure you can live with it or have a plan to fix it.
  7. Check for any transfer credit that should be there but is missing.
  8. Give it a vibe check for anything that feels off from your lived experience.

Part 2 — Reflection (answer all prompts)

In 5–10 sentences total, answer:

  1. What surprised you when you looked at your transcript?
  2. What’s one thing you’re proud of so far?
  3. What’s one thing you want to improve this semester (study habits, attendance, time management, asking for help, etc.)
  4. Any issues to flag (missing credit, repeated course, transfer credit weirdness, hold, incorrect grade posting)?

If you spot something that looks wrong, that’s not “bad news”—that’s useful intel. Bring it up early so we can fix it.

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your transcript anywhere public (GitHub, Discord, etc.)
  • Submit only through Canvas
  • If your transcript contains sensitive information (it often does), keep it private and don’t share it with classmates

Grading / rubric (10 points)

  • 4 pts — Transcript PDF submitted, readable, correct document
  • 4 pts — Reflection answers all prompts with real effort (not one-word responses)
  • 2 pts — File naming + submission is clean and on time

Common problems + fixes

  • “I can’t find the transcript option.”
    Try searching in Self-Service for: transcript and look for “unofficial transcript”.

  • “My transcript looks wrong.”
    Submit what you can and mention the issue in your reflection. We’ll handle it together.

  • “I have a hold and can’t access it.”
    Submit a screenshot of the hold message (if allowed) and write what happened in the reflection.

Notes (instructor)

  • This pairs with A02 (Progress Report) and A03 (Degree Plan).
  • Goal: Know what it takes to graduate: identify issues early + start planning with accurate data.

A02 — Progress report

Why we’re doing this

Your Progress Report (from the registrar) is the closest thing to “the truth in writing” about your degree requirements. It shows what you’ve completed, what still remains, and where your gaps are. This assignment makes sure you know how to find it and how to read it. The same software that does your graduation check does your progress report.

What you will submit

Submit two items:

1) Progress Report PDF - Export your Progress Report from Self-Service as a PDF.

2) Short summary - Submit a short written summary (either Canvas text entry or a second page in the same PDF).

File naming (PDF)

Name your PDF: - CS1_A02_ProgressReport_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf

Example: - CS1_A02_ProgressReport_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf

Step-by-step instructions (how to get the report)

  1. Log in to SWOSU Single Sign-On.
  2. Open Self-Service (same ecosystem where you access other student tools).
  3. Search for: Progress Report
  4. Open your report and export/download as PDF.
  5. Save it somewhere you can find again (you’ll use it again for A01).

Summary requirements (your written part)

Write 6–10 sentences that answer these prompts:

1) What degree/major does the Progress Report show?
2) What areas/categories are listed? (Gen Ed, major core, electives, etc.)
3) List 3 specific requirements you still need (courses or requirement blocks).
4) Identify 1 thing that surprised you (or one part you don’t understand yet).
5) What’s your next step? (Example: “I need to ask an advisor about ” or “I need to plan when I’ll take .”)

If something looks wrong

If anything seems incorrect or missing, say so in your summary and include the exact section name you’re referencing. Don’t panic — just document it.

Grading / rubric (10 points)

  • Progress Report PDF successfully submitted: 3
  • Summary meets requirements (prompts answered, complete, clear): 5
  • Specificity (real requirement names / real sections, not vague): 2

Need help?

If you can’t find the report or something looks unexpected, message me on Canvas or email: - [redacted-instructor-email]

Upload one PDF that was exported from a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

File naming

Name your file: - CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf

Example: - CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fa.pdf

Requirements (what must be in your spreadsheet)

1) Title + basics (top of page)

Include: - Your name - Major (and minor if applicable) - Option (if applicable) - Your expected graduation semester (example: “Spring 2028”)

2) Semester-by-semester plan (the main table)

Your plan must list every semester from now until graduation.

For each planned course, include: - Course prefix/number (example: CS 1033) - Course name (example: “Computer Science I”) - Credits - Notes (optional but encouraged: “needs prereq,” “only offered fall,” etc.)

For each semester, include: - Total credits that semester

3) Prerequisites + reality check

Somewhere on the sheet (or in a notes area), show evidence that you checked: - SWOSU course catalog / schedule offerings (when courses are typically offered) - Your progress report (what requirements remain) - Your unofficial transcript (what you already completed)

This can be: - A short “checked list” section - Notes in a dedicated column - A small “Verification” box

4) Two scenarios (minimum)

Include at least two graduation scenarios, such as: - Scenario A: ~12 credits/semester - Scenario B: ~18 credits/semester with summer classes

For each scenario, clearly show: - Expected graduation term - What changes between the two plans (credit load / summer / specific course shifts)

5) Advising notes / questions

Include a short list of questions or notes for an advisor (minimum 2 items), like: - “Is Course X offered every spring?” - “Do I need an elective in category Y?” - “Does internship credit apply to requirement Z?”

Step-by-step instructions (how to build it)

  1. Open Excel or Google Sheets.
  2. Create a sheet named: Degree Plan
  3. Add your title + graduation target at the top.
  4. Build your main table: - Suggested columns: Semester | Course # | Course Name | Credits | Notes
  5. Add semester totals (a SUM at the bottom of each semester block is perfect).
  6. Duplicate the sheet (or create a second section) for Scenario B.
  7. Export as PDF: - Excel: File → Export → Create PDF - Google Sheets: File → Download → PDF

Grading / rubric (20 points)

  • Completeness of plan (all semesters + courses listed to graduation): 6
  • Accuracy & realism (credits, prereqs considered, offerings checked): 6
  • Two scenarios included + clearly explained: 4
  • Clarity & organization (readable, labeled, totals included): 3
  • Correct submission format + filename: 1

Late / revision notes

If something doesn’t make sense (missing prereqs, unsure offering), mark it clearly as a question — don’t guess silently. Planning is allowed to be imperfect; hiding uncertainty is not.

Need help?

If anything looks unexpected in your progress report or transcript, message me on Canvas or email: - [redacted-instructor-email]

assignments.description:
Resume (Professional Artifact + Evidence Pack)

A04 — Resume (Professional Artifact + Evidence Pack)

Due: SET_THIS

P01 — Resume (Professional Artifact + Evidence Pack)

Your resume is not a history report. It’s a marketing document with one purpose:

To convince a hiring manager to interview you.

This assignment is a full professional build: you will create a resume that follows modern best practices, targets a real job or internship, and includes an “evidence pack” proving your claims are real and intentional.

What you will submit (Canvas)

Submit THREE files:

1) Resume PDF
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_Resume.pdf

2) Evidence Pack (PDF)
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_EvidencePack.pdf

3) Reflection + Revision Log (PDF or Markdown)
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_RevisionLog.pdf (or .md)

Part A — Choose a target (required)

Pick one real posting you could qualify for within 0–3 years: - internship / student worker / entry-level job

In your Revision Log, include: - Job title + company - A link to the posting (or a screenshot if needed) - 5 keywords or skill phrases from the posting

Example keywords: - “customer service” - “Python” - “troubleshooting” - “team collaboration” - “documentation” - “data analysis” - “networking basics” - “Excel / spreadsheets” - “public speaking” - “project management”

Part B — Resume requirements (you must meet these)

1) Format and structure rules (non-negotiable)

  • 1 page (unless you have 10+ years of relevant experience—rare)
  • Single-column layout (ATS-friendly; avoid multi-column templates)
  • Consistent spacing, fonts, and alignment
  • Clear section headings (as applicable):
  • Education, Experience, Projects, Skills, Certifications/Awards
  • Bullet points (not paragraphs) for Experience/Projects

2) Required sections

Your resume must include:

Header - Name - City/State - Phone - Professional email - LinkedIn URL (or “LinkedIn: In progress” if not yet created)

Education - School, degree/major (or intended major), expected graduation date - GPA optional (include only if strong and accurate)

Experience You must include at least one: - job, volunteer role, internship, leadership role, or meaningful responsibility

Projects You must include at least one project (class, personal, club, work).
Projects count even if you think they’re “small.”

Skills - 8–16 skills, grouped into categories - Example: Languages, Tools, Concepts, Professional Skills

3) Bullet point quality rules (this is where you earn points)

You must write: - 8–12 bullets total across Experience + Projects
- At least 6 bullets must follow this formula:

Action Verb + What you did + How you did it + Result/Impact

Strong bullet examples (copy the pattern, not the content)

  • Improved a spreadsheet-based inventory tracker by automating formulas and validation, reducing data entry errors from frequent mistakes to rare ones.
  • Built a Python program that parses and summarizes text files using functions and loops; delivered results in a clean table format.
  • Led a 4-person lab team by assigning roles and setting checkpoints, finishing 2 days early with all requirements met.
  • Resolved customer issues by asking diagnostic questions and documenting outcomes, maintaining positive feedback (use numbers if you have them).

Weak bullet examples (avoid these)

  • “Responsible for helping customers.”
  • “Worked on a project in class.”
  • “Did programming in Python.”
  • “Good communication skills.”

4) Proof and credibility rules

  • No inflated titles, no fake metrics, no “expert” if you’re not.
  • If you use numbers, they must be real or clearly described as approximate.
  • Every bullet should be something you can explain out loud.

Part C — Evidence Pack (this is how you prove it)

Create a PDF with evidence backing your resume claims.

Include at least 6 items, chosen from below (mix is encouraged): - Screenshot of a project README, GitHub repo page, or code snippet - Photo of a poster/presentation you made - Screenshot of a spreadsheet/dashboard you built - Certificate (LinkedIn Learning, etc.) - Email or note showing recognition (blur names if needed) - A short “before/after” example of something you improved - A work sample excerpt (documentation, tutorial you wrote, lab report section)

Rules: - If it’s sensitive, blur/black out private info. - The Evidence Pack must have a table of contents: - Item #, title, and which resume bullet it supports (e.g., “Supports Bullet 3”)

Part D — Reflection + revision log (required)

In 1–2 pages total, answer:

1) Your resume’s message (the “headline”)
In one sentence: What do you want a hiring manager to believe about you?
Example: “I’m a reliable early-career tech professional who learns fast, communicates clearly, and finishes projects.”

2) Your best 3 bullets and why they’re strong
Explain using the formula: action + method + impact.

3) Your weakest section and your plan to strengthen it
Be specific: “Add a second project,” “Join Computer Club,” “Complete a certificate,” etc.

4) Revision record
- Include two rounds of revision - Describe what changed each time (formatting, verbs, metrics, clarity) - If you used AI: state how you used it (example: “I used AI to rewrite bullets, then edited to match my real experience.”)

AI / internet tools policy (allowed—with ownership)

You may use AI/LLMs and online examples to: - generate bullet drafts - reword for clarity - suggest formats or action verbs

But: - Your resume must be accurate and personal - If asked, you must be able to explain or edit any bullet - Generic, copy-paste-looking content will lose points on quality

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your resume publicly (GitHub, Discord, etc.) unless you intentionally choose to later
  • Do not include sensitive info (SSN, full address, birthdate, etc.)
  • Submit only through Canvas

Grading rubric (Likert-style) — 100 points total

How grading works: Each category below is scored 0–4 based on the descriptors.
Points are then calculated using the category weight.

Category points = (score ÷ 4) × category weight

Example: If “Bullet Quality” is weight 30 and the student earns a 3:
(3/4) × 30 = 22.5 points.

1) Format + ATS readiness (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
1 page, single-column, clean headings, consistent spacing/fonts, no clutter. Reads easily in 10 seconds. ATS-friendly.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
Mostly clean and readable; minor formatting issues (slightly inconsistent spacing, headings, or alignment) but still ATS-friendly.

2 — Some (7.5):
Formatting distracts from content: inconsistent headings/spacing, dense sections, awkward layout. Still readable but not professional.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Hard to read or clearly not ATS-friendly: multi-column template, tiny font, clutter, or confusing organization.

0 — No credit (0):
Not submitted, not a resume, or unreadable file.

2) Targeting to a real posting (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
Posting link (or screenshot) included; 5 keywords listed; resume clearly reflects the posting (skills/bullets aligned).

3 — Mostly (11.25):
Posting + keywords included; some alignment, but targeting is uneven (keywords don’t show up in bullets/skills strongly).

2 — Some (7.5):
Posting OR keywords are weak/missing detail; resume looks generic; minimal connection to the job requirements.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Posting is unclear/unrelated; keywords missing; targeting not attempted.

0 — No credit (0):
No posting and no keywords; completely ignores this requirement.

3) Required sections complete (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
Header, Education, Experience, Projects, Skills all present and meaningful. Skills are grouped and specific.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
All sections present but one is thin (e.g., projects vague or skills not grouped) OR minor missing detail.

2 — Some (7.5):
One required section missing OR multiple sections are too thin/vague to be useful.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Two+ required sections missing; looks incomplete or rushed.

0 — No credit (0):
Not a resume or not submitted.

4) Bullet quality + best practices (Weight: 30)

4 — Full credit (30):
8–12 bullets total. At least 6 bullets follow Action + Method + Impact. Strong verbs, specific tools, no filler. Bullets are believable and clear.

3 — Mostly (22.5):
Meets bullet count; several strong bullets, but impact/method is missing in a few. Some generic wording remains.

2 — Some (15):
Bullets exist but many are weak (“responsible for,” vague duties, no tools, no outcomes). Less than 6 strong-formula bullets.

1 — Not yet (7.5):
Few bullets, mostly vague or task-only statements. Little evidence of best practices.

0 — No credit (0):
No bullets, or bullet content is clearly unrelated / copied without understanding.

5) Evidence Pack quality + mapping (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
6+ evidence items, table of contents included, each item clearly maps to a resume bullet (“supports bullet #”). Evidence is relevant and professional.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
6 items present with a TOC, but mapping is sometimes unclear OR some items are weak evidence.

2 — Some (7.5):
Fewer than 6 items OR missing TOC OR mapping to bullets is inconsistent/confusing.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Evidence pack is mostly filler, unrelated, or not clearly connected to resume claims.

0 — No credit (0):
No evidence pack submitted.

6) Reflection + revision log (Weight: 10)

4 — Full credit (10):
Includes: resume “message” sentence, best 3 bullets explained using best-practice logic, weakest section + plan, and two revision rounds described. If AI used, explains how.

3 — Mostly (7.5):
Covers most requirements; missing one piece (e.g., only one revision round or weak explanation of bullet strength).

2 — Some (5):
Reflection is brief or generic; revision details unclear; missing multiple required parts.

1 — Not yet (2.5):
Minimal effort; doesn’t demonstrate understanding of what was improved and why.

0 — No credit (0):
Not submitted.

LLM-friendly feedback format (optional but recommended)

When giving feedback, include: 1) Category scores (0–4)
2) 2–3 bullets of “what you did well”
3) 2–3 bullets of “highest-impact fixes next”
4) Rewrite one weak bullet into a strong bullet (Action + Method + Impact)

Suggested Canvas settings (edit if needed)

  • Available: Week 2 Monday, 12:00am (suggestion)
  • Due: Week 2 Thursday, 5:00pm (suggestion)
  • Until: End of semester, 11:59pm
  • Points: 100
  • Submission type: File upload (PDFs) + file upload or text entry for Revision Log

assignments.description:
Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

A05 — Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

Due: SET_THIS

P02 — Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

This is the professional mirror of the degree-plan work you did at the start of the semester.

  • Your resume = your “unofficial transcript” (what’s true today)
  • Your dream job report = your professional “degree plan” (where you want to go and what that role actually requires)

Goal: Identify a real role you want to grow into, understand what it demands, and explain why it matters to you. This is not fantasy — it’s future planning.

Why this assignment exists (read this first)

A dream job report is a motivation engine and a navigation map.

  • It helps you decide what you’re aiming at (so you don’t wander for four years and then wonder why job searching feels impossible).
  • It turns “someday” into a concrete target: responsibilities, tools, expectations, and what success looks like.
  • It becomes the foundation for the next assignment: your Gap Analysis (what you still need and how you’ll build it).

Important mindset: This is a target, not a judgment.
You are not expected to be ready for this job today. You are expected to be honest, specific, and intentional.

Also: this is one of the few assignments that is primarily about you — it’s designed to be private and personally useful.

What you will submit (Canvas)

Submit using TWO Canvas submission parts:

Part 1 — File Upload (required)

Upload TWO PDFs:

1) Dream Job Report (PDF)
Filename: A05_Lastname_Firstname_DreamJobReport.pdf

2) Job Posting Snapshot + Source List (PDF)
Filename: A05_Lastname_Firstname_JobSources.pdf

Part 2 — Text Entry (required)

Paste the full text of your Dream Job Report into the Canvas Text Entry box.

Why this is required: PDF is a layout format and sometimes text can be extracted in weird order by automated tools. Pasting the text ensures you get the best possible feedback from automated review tools and makes your submission easier to read and review.

(Yes — you still upload the PDF. The Text Entry is for clean text and feedback.)

LLM-friendly formatting rules (required)

To make your PDF readable to both humans and automated tools:

  • Use a single-column layout
  • Avoid text boxes, sidebars, and fancy templates
  • Keep tables short (a small table is fine; don’t put your whole report in a table)
  • Export a normal PDF with selectable text (not a scanned image)

Part A — Pick a real dream job + a realistic backup (required)

Choose one specific job title you would be excited to hold in 5–10 years.

Also choose a backup plan role (Plan B) that still interests you and is closer to entry-level.

Rules for job selection

  • It must be a real job title found in real postings (company site, LinkedIn, Indeed, USAJobs, etc.).
  • “Entrepreneur / business owner” is not a job title for this assignment.
    If your dream is to run a business, choose the functional role you would do most days.

Examples: - Founder — Engineering Lead - Founder — Product & Sales - Founder — Operations / Finance - Founder — Cybersecurity Consultant

Your responsibilities/tools/metrics must match that function (no fluffy “I will inspire people” job descriptions — real work only).

Part B — Collect evidence (required sources)

You must use at least 3 credible sources.
At least 1 source must be from this “high-trust” list: - BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook (OOH) (government career profiles: duties, environment, education/training, pay, outlook) - USAJOBS (official federal job postings) - An official company job posting (company careers page)

Other credible sources you may use: - Professional organizations (ACM, IEEE, ISACA, etc.) - Certification providers (CompTIA, Cisco, AWS, Microsoft, PMI, etc.) - University career services pages - Handshake/LinkedIn Learning course pages (as supporting info)

Your JobSources PDF must include

  • 1–2 job postings (screenshots or saved PDFs)
  • A source list with working links AND a 1–2 sentence note describing what each source contributed

Citations (simple, consistent)

Use any citation style you want (APA/MLA/Chicago/etc.), but be consistent.
At minimum, include working links and source notes.

Part C — Write your Dream Job Report (main deliverable)

Length: 2–3 pages (double-spaced)
Format: 12 pt font, 1-inch margins, clear section headings
Tone: professional but personal — this should motivate you

Use the headings below in this order.

1) Job Identity (who/what/where)

Include: - Dream Job Title (Plan A) - Backup Job Title (Plan B) - Typical industries or employers - Work setting (remote/on-site/hybrid, team size, environment) - A 3–5 sentence “day-in-the-life” summary (based on sources)

2) Job Description (what you actually do)

Write a job description in your own words (not copied). Include:

  • 6–10 core responsibilities
  • 5 key tools/technologies (or methods) used in the role
  • 3 success metrics (how performance is measured)

Examples of success metrics (pick ones that fit your role): - “Reduce incidents / downtime” - “Deliver features on schedule” - “Improve performance by X%” - “Customer satisfaction / ticket resolution time” - “Accuracy / error rate / reliability” - “Security findings reduced / compliance maintained”

3) Requirements Map (what the job expects)

Create a simple table (include in your report):

Requirement Type Plan A: What the job requires Evidence/source
Education
Technical Skills
Professional Skills
Experience
Certifications (if relevant)

Then add a second mini-table for Plan B:

Requirement Type Plan B: What the job requires Evidence/source
Education
Technical Skills
Professional Skills
Experience
Certifications (if relevant)

4) Why this is your dream job (the motivation engine)

Answer honestly: - Why does this role excite you? - What problems do you want to solve? - What impact do you want to have (people, community, business, science, etc.)?

Reminder: This is a target, not a judgment. Be real. Be specific.

5) Fit Check (what you already have + what you still need)

Write two short lists for Plan A:

Already building (at least 5 items):
Skills, strengths, experiences, habits, or values you already have that support this path.

Still need to build (at least 5 items):
Skills, credentials, experiences, or habits you must develop to be competitive.

Then add a short note: - Which gaps overlap between Plan A and Plan B? - Which gaps are unique to Plan A?

6) How you combined sources (anti-copy/paste paragraph)

Write a short paragraph (5–8 sentences) answering: - Which sources you used - What each source helped you understand - How you combined them into your own job description and requirements map

This is a simple way to show honest effort and reduce accidental copy/paste.

7) Your 12-month action plan (first step toward the future)

Create a concrete plan with 8–12 actions you can take in the next year.

Your plan must include: - 2 actions related to coursework - 2 actions related to projects/portfolio - 2 actions related to professional networking or involvement (club, event, mentorship, etc.) - 1 action related to communication (writing, speaking, presenting, interviewing) - 1 action related to skill-building (course/certification/self-study)

Make each action specific (recommended format): - Verb + artifact + deadline
Examples: - “Build a small data project and publish a README by April 1.” - “Attend one Computer Club meeting and introduce myself to 2 members by Feb 15.” - “Complete one LinkedIn Learning course on interviewing by March 10.”

Put your plan in checklist format and include a timeline (this semester / summer / next fall).

AI / internet tools policy (allowed — with ownership)

You may use AI/LLMs to: - help outline your report - improve clarity and writing - summarize sources (then verify)

But: - You must write in your own voice - Do not copy job postings word-for-word - If your report reads generic or source-copied, you will lose points on quality - You should be able to explain your choices and revise a section if asked

Grading rubric (Likert-style) — 100 points total

How grading works: Each category is scored 0–4.
Points = (score ÷ 4) × category weight.

1) Job selection + clarity (Plan A + Plan B) (Weight: 15)

4: Plan A and Plan B are real, specific roles; time horizon makes sense; titles are precise and consistent; founder roles have clear functional focus.
3: Roles are real but slightly vague or Plan B is weakly defined.
2: Role selection is fuzzy, inconsistent, or unrealistic; Plan B unclear.
1: Very vague (“work with computers”), unclear roles or missing Plan B.
0: Not real job titles / off-task.

2) Evidence + source quality (Weight: 20)

4: 3+ credible sources; includes 1–2 postings; includes at least 1 high-trust source; clear source notes; evidence supports claims.
3: Sources credible but notes are thin OR postings missing one required item OR high-trust source is present but weakly used.
2: Weak sources or unclear contributions; postings limited; high-trust requirement barely met.
1: Minimal sources; credibility concerns; little evidence used.
0: No sources / missing JobSources PDF.

3) Job description quality (responsibilities/tools/metrics) (Weight: 20)

4: Responsibilities/tools/metrics are specific, accurate, and clearly written in student’s own words; reads like a real job.
3: Mostly specific; some vague items; metrics/tools not strongly connected.
2: Generic description; unclear responsibilities; tools/metrics weak.
1: Mostly copied tone or very unclear.
0: Missing.

4) Requirements Map quality (Plan A + Plan B) (Weight: 15)

4: Both tables complete; evidence column filled; covers education, tech/pro skills, experience, certs (if relevant).
3: Both tables present but evidence is weak for some items OR one table thinner.
2: Tables incomplete or too generic; missing categories or evidence.
1: Bare minimum effort; not useful.
0: Missing.

5) Motivation + personal connection (Weight: 15)

4: Authentic, specific, meaningful; connects values, impact, and reasons clearly; motivating to read.
3: Personal connection present but could be deeper or more specific.
2: Generic motivation; limited reflection.
1: Minimal personal connection.
0: Missing.

6) Fit Check + reflection on gaps (Weight: 5)

4: 5+ items in each list; thoughtful; clearly identifies overlap vs unique gaps.
3: Lists complete but somewhat generic; overlap/unique note thin.
2: Lists too short or vague; weak analysis.
1: Minimal effort.
0: Missing.

7) Source-combination paragraph (Weight: 5)

4: Clearly explains how sources were combined; shows honest synthesis; reduces copy/paste risk.
3: Present but shallow; limited synthesis detail.
2: Very brief; unclear how sources were used.
1: Minimal effort.
0: Missing.

8) 12-month action plan quality (Weight: 15)

4: 8–12 actions; meets all required categories; includes timeline; actions are concrete (verb + artifact + deadline).
3: Meets most requirements; a few actions vague or missing one category/timeline detail.
2: Too few actions; vague; missing multiple categories.
1: Minimal plan; not actionable.
0: Missing.

Submission checklist

Before submitting, confirm: - [ ] Report is 2–3 pages, double-spaced, with the required headings (in order) - [ ] Both Requirements Map tables are included and filled out with evidence - [ ] Source-combination paragraph is included - [ ] 12-month action plan includes 8–12 concrete actions + timeline - [ ] JobSources PDF includes 1–2 postings + 3+ sources + notes + at least 1 high-trust source - [ ] You uploaded PDFs AND pasted your report text into the Canvas Text Entry box

Suggested Canvas settings (edit if needed)

  • Available: Week 3 Monday, 12:00am (suggestion)
  • Due: Week 3 Thursday, 5:00pm (suggestion)
  • Until: End of semester, 11:59pm
  • Points: 100
  • Submission type: File upload + Text Entry
